content: Breastfeeding counseling is designed to meet the specific needs of each individual and is offered with sensitivity, taking into account the mother’s social and cultural background. The guideline development group concluded that the benefits of breastfeeding counseling significantly outweigh any potential harms. This conclusion applies universally to all aspects of breastfeeding counseling, whether it is provided during the antenatal period, postnatally, or both, regardless of the frequency, mode of delivery (face-to-face or remote), or the type of health worker (lay or non-lay) involved. This principle will not be reiterated in subsequent discussions of key questions. A systematic review of qualitative studies on mothers’ values and preferences regarding breastfeeding counseling consistently revealed that women desire more counseling and emphasize the importance of follow-up. Counseling, whether provided or actively sought by women, is highly valued and associated with high satisfaction levels. The evidence supporting this is of high confidence. Variability in values and preferences was considered minor, although cultural differences in the value placed on breastfeeding may influence the perceived importance of breastfeeding counseling. A systematic review of qualitative studies among key stakeholders demonstrated that breastfeeding counseling is highly valued. However, it was acknowledged that health workers might hesitate to provide counseling if they are not adequately trained or allocated sufficient time for counseling. The evidence supporting this is of high confidence. Variability in the acceptability of counseling was judged to be minor, although implementation challenges were considered significant in determining acceptability. The guideline development group agreed that implementing breastfeeding counseling interventions for pregnant women and mothers will require additional resources, which will vary depending on the context. These resources may include indirect or opportunity costs for health-care workers, women, and their families due to the time spent in counseling. There was insufficient data to accurately estimate these costs. However, the group suggested that breastfeeding counseling interventions likely constitute a significant component of breastfeeding intervention packages, which are already widely implemented. Given the shortand long-term benefits of breastfeeding on child survival, health, and development, as well as maternal health benefits, providing counseling that likely impacts breastfeeding practices may be highly cost-effective. The group also agreed that equity will be enhanced if quality counseling is widely accessible to all pregnant women and mothers. If counseling is available but only accessible to women in well-resourced settings or those who can afford private services, equity may be reduced, favoring high-income families or countries. Conversely, in some contexts, women from higher wealth quintiles and high-income countries may be targeted with competing messages that undermine optimal breastfeeding practices and promote breast-milk substitutes. This underscores the importance of ensuring that quality breastfeeding counseling is accessible to all pregnant women and mothers to promote equity. The group determined that counseling all pregnant women and mothers is feasible, given available resources (human, financial, and organizational). According to the Global Nutrition Policy Review 2016–2017, 99% of the 161 countries surveyed reported implementing breastfeeding counseling in 2016. To enable quality counseling, appropriate training or coaching of health workers and lay/non-lay counselors by skilled trainers is essential. Trained counselors need sufficient time for counseling, and innovative solutions at the systems level, such as cascade capacity-building approaches, will be required to facilitate appropriate breastfeeding counseling. The recommendation is that breastfeeding counseling should be provided to all pregnant women and mothers with young children. This recommendation is based on moderate-quality evidence. Breastfeeding counseling is a process and interaction between counselors and pregnant women or mothers. It is not intended to be a “top-down” intervention where women are told what to do. Instead, the aim is to empower women to breastfeed while respecting their personal situations and wishes. Breastfeeding counseling is never forced upon any woman, as this would contradict the concept of counseling. Rather, it is made available and accessible to all pregnant women and mothers, particularly those considering or already breastfeeding. Breastfeeding counseling for pregnant women can help them establish a strong foundation for breastfeeding, supporting mothers and their neonates to initiate breastfeeding as soon as possible after birth, remain together day and night, and establish and maintain breastfeeding with proper attachment and positioning. Sensitive and effective counseling can assist mothers who are considering or already breastfeeding to overcome challenges. By emphasizing that breastfeeding provides protection, comfort, and nourishment, counseling can address the specific barriers individual mothers face. Mothers who may not be considering breastfeeding can be supported to make informed choices about feeding their infants and children. Counseling can highlight the extensive and well-documented benefits of breastfeeding while providing mothers with scientific, unbiased, and factual information about other infant and young child feeding options, enabling them to feed their children safely and responsively. Mothers who are breastfeeding while also providing additional foods or fluids (such as infant formula milk or other breast-milk substitutes) are encouraged to continue breastfeeding as much as they are able. They should be supported with sensitivity and care to address any challenges they may face regarding feeding their child. The timing of breastfeeding counseling, whether antenatal, postnatal, or both, was evaluated. Evidence suggests that antenatal counseling may reduce the likelihood of not breastfeeding within one hour after birth compared to standard care or no counseling. However, there is limited evidence on the impact of postnatal counseling alone. Counseling during both periods may reduce the likelihood of not breastfeeding at 4–6 weeks postpartum compared to standard care or no counseling. Counseling also likely reduces the use of artificial teats and bottles. The guideline development group emphasized the importance of providing breastfeeding counseling to all pregnant women and mothers to improve breastfeeding practices. This recommendation is informed by evidence and explicit consideration of factors such as the quality of evidence, balance of benefits and harms, values and preferences, acceptability, resource implications, equity, and feasibility.
